:::{#exr-compute-surv-pred}

#### Construct a prediction interval

```{r}
#| include: false
mu = 7
```

Suppose a cancer patient is predicted to have an [expected (mean)](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-expectation) lifetime of 
`r mu` years after diagnosis, and suppose the distribution is exponential.

Construct a 95% [prediction interval](https://morrison-lab.github.io/sds/intro-MLEs.html#def-prediction-interval) for survival.

:::

:::{.callout-tip}

Use the [quantiles](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-quantile-function) of the exponential distribution.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#sol-compute-surv-pred}

If the mean is `r mu` years until death, 
then the rate parameter $\haz = 1/`r mu`$ events (deaths) per year.

The 0.025 quantile of the exponential distribution with $\haz = 1/`r mu`$ is 
``qexp(p 0.025, rate = 1/`r mu`)`` = `r qexp(0.025, rate = 1/mu)` 
and the 0.975 quantile is 
``qexp(p 0.975, rate = 1/`r mu`)`` = `r qexp(0.975, rate = 1/mu)`, 
so the prediction interval is 
``qexp(p c(.025, 0.975), rate = 1/`r mu`)`` = (`r qexp(c(.025, 0.975), rate = 1/mu)`).
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#exr-graph-prediction-intervals}
Graph the prediction interval as a function of the mean,
for [Gaussian](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-normal) ($\sigma = 1$), [Binomial](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/distributions.html#def-binomial), [Poisson](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/distributions.html#def-poisson), and [Exponential](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-exponential).
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exr-explain-surv-pred}
#### Explain the results

Why do time-to-event models have such wide predictive intervals?

:::

:::{.callout-tip}

Consider the relationship between the mean, [variance](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/variance-covariance.html#def-variance), and [standard deviation](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/variance-covariance.html#def-sd) of the exponential distribution, and contrast that relationship with the [Poisson distribution](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/distributions.html#def-poisson) and the [Bernoulli distribution](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-bernoulli).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#sol-explain-surv-pred}

In the exponential distribution, variance is the square of the mean (hence SD is equal to mean); 
as opposed to Poisson, 
where variance was equal to the mean 
(and SD is the square-root of the mean), 
or the Bernoulli, 
where the variance is the mean minus the square of the mean (so the SD is smaller than the square-root of the mean).

:::
